summary: Defines the DHCP Relay Agent Information option, which lets a relay add details such as where a request came from before passing it to a server. Operators of shared access networks can use this to apply their own policies and protect against some abuse. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A mail clerk who passes your request along can stamp it with which door it came through. This lets a network helper add that note.

subtitle: How a relay agent tags DHCP requests with where they came from, so servers can apply policy and resist spoofing.

tldr.problem: When many untrusted customer hosts get addresses through DHCP over shared circuits, the server cannot tell which circuit or modem a request came from, which opens the door to address exhaustion and spoofing.
tldr.mechanism: The relay agent, which sits in the trusted circuit access equipment, adds a Relay Agent Information option (code 82) holding sub-options such as a circuit ID and a remote ID. The server echoes it back and the relay strips it before the reply reaches the client.
tldr.outcome: Servers can assign addresses and apply limits per circuit or per remote ID. The design only works when the relay agent, the server and the network between them are trusted. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 6607.

today: RFC 3046 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 6607. Nothing in the unit metadata says it has been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Problem on Shared Access Networks
sections.content:
Public Internet access often runs over a circuit access unit that connects many users through switched or permanent circuits (ISDN, ATM, Frame Relay, cable data and similar). Newer high-speed circuits frequently give the customer a LAN interface for one or more hosts, and it is attractive to assign those hosts addresses centrally with DHCP as defined in RFC 2131.

A router at the customer site would need its own address and a dedicated logical IP subnet for each user, which the RFC calls unsuitable for large public networks. So the circuit access unit acts as both router and DHCP relay agent. This lets DHCP broadcast replies be sent only to the right circuit instead of being copied onto thousands of circuits.

The RFC lists the security questions that arise with untrusted clients: how to prevent DHCP address exhaustion (an attacker requests every address using fabricated client MAC addresses), how to give an address or subnet permanently to one user or modem, and how to stop spoofing of client identifier fields and of other clients' MAC addresses. The answer is to let the trusted circuit access equipment add information to the requests it forwards.
sections.eli5: Lots of houses share one post office. The post office worker knows which house each letter came from, but the sorting room does not. So the worker writes the house number on each letter.

sections.title: The Relay Agent Information Option
sections.content:
The new DHCP option is a container with option code 82 and a length N giving the number of octets in the Agent Information field. That field is a sequence of sub-option tuples, each made of a sub-option code, a length and a value.

There is no pad sub-option, and the field must not be ended with a 255 sub-option. The length N covers every byte of all the sub-option tuples, while each sub-option's own length counts only its value. At least one sub-option must be present, so the minimum length is two. A sub-option length may be zero, and sub-options need not appear in code order.

The initial sub-options are 1 (Agent Circuit ID) and 2 (Agent Remote ID). Packing everything into one option with sub-options was deliberate: any future mechanism that authenticates DHCP between client and server can then leave this single option out of its calculation.
sections.eli5: It is a labelled box with smaller labelled envelopes inside. Each envelope has a number that says what kind of note it holds and how long the note is.

sections.title: What the Relay Agent Does
sections.content:
Adding the option SHOULD be configurable and SHOULD be off by default, with a separate setting for each sub-option. When a relay agent adds the option to a BOOTP or DHCP packet going from client to server, it SHALL put it last, just before the End option (255) if one is present.

If a packet arrives from an untrusted circuit with giaddr set to zero (so this agent is the first-hop router) but already carries a Relay Agent Information option, the agent SHALL discard it and increment an error count. A trusted circuit may contain a trusted downstream element, such as a bridge, that adds its own option. In that case the relay does not add a second one. How circuits are classed as trusted or untrusted depends on the equipment. For example, a cable modem termination system may treat most cable modems as untrusted, while an ATM switch behind a DSLAM may treat its circuits as trusted.

Other rules protect the packet:

  • An optional maximum packet size may be configured. If adding the option would exceed it, the packet is forwarded without the option and an error counter SHOULD be incremented. Without that setting, the agent SHALL NOT grow a packet past the interface MTU.
  • The agent SHALL NOT use an Option Overload option or the file or sname fields for the option.
  • The option echoed by a server MUST be removed before the reply is forwarded to the client.
  • Relays are not required to watch unicast packets sent straight to the server, such as the DHCP-REQUEST sent when renewing.
  • Relays MUST NOT modify packets that use the IPSEC Authentication Header or Encapsulating Security Payload.

When a packet comes from another relay closer to the client, with a nonzero giaddr, the agent discards it if the giaddr spoofs one of its own addresses. Otherwise it forwards the packet without adding options and without changing giaddr.
sections.eli5: The clerk adds the note only if the boss allows it, never opens a letter that is already stamped by an outsider, and takes the stamp off the reply before giving it back.

sections.title: What the Server Does
sections.content:
A server that does not know the option ignores it and does not echo it, which is the normal handling of unknown options. A server that claims to support it SHALL echo the entire option in all replies, and SHOULD copy it as the last option in the response. It SHALL NOT put the echo in the overloaded sname or file fields.

If the server cannot fit the full option into a reply, it SHALL send the reply without it and SHOULD increment an error counter. Because relays may choose to watch unicast messages and add the option, servers SHOULD be ready to see it in unicast messages but MUST NOT expect it always to be there.
sections.eli5: The server reads the stamp, then copies it onto its answer exactly as it was so the clerk knows where to send the reply.

sections.title: The Circuit ID and Remote ID Sub-options
sections.content:
The Agent Circuit ID (sub-option 1) MAY be added by relays that terminate switched or permanent circuits. It is an agent-local identifier of the circuit a request arrived on. The RFC suggests a router interface number, a switching hub port, a Remote Access Server port, a Frame Relay DLCI, or an ATM or cable data virtual circuit number. Relays use it to send replies back to the right circuit. Servers MAY use it for address and parameter policy, SHOULD treat it as an opaque value matched exactly, and SHOULD NOT parse it. Since it is only meaningful to one relay, it should be qualified with the giaddr identifying that relay.

The Agent Remote ID (sub-option 2) MAY be added by relays that can identify the remote end of the circuit. Examples include a caller ID phone number, a user name prompted for by a Remote Access Server, a remote ATM address, a cable modem ID, the remote IP address of a point-to-point link, or a remote X.25 address. The remote ID MUST be globally unique. Servers MAY use it to choose parameters for particular users, hosts or modems, and SHOULD treat it as opaque. A relay MAY use it, in addition to or instead of the circuit ID, to pick the circuit for a reply.
sections.eli5: The circuit ID says which door the letter came through. The remote ID says who the sender is, like a name tag that cannot be faked.

sections.title: Problems Solved and Security Limits
sections.content:
The RFC states what the option fixes, assuming all public DHCP traffic goes through the relay and the network between relay and server is uncompromised:

  • Broadcast forwarding: replies go only on the circuit named by the circuit ID.
  • Address exhaustion: a server can track the triplet of client IP address, client MAC address and remote ID, and SHOULD limit the number of addresses given to one remote ID.
  • Static assignment: a server can tie addresses to particular remote IDs and refuse unauthorized ones.
  • IP spoofing: the access device MAY block packets whose source address is not one it associated with that circuit.
  • Client identifier spoofing: the server need not use the untrusted client identifier field.
  • MAC address spoofing: binding a MAC address to a remote ID lets the server avoid offering an address to an attacker using the same MAC on a different remote ID.

The security model relies on an implied trust between relay agent and server and treats the client as untrusted. The relay agent, the server and the whole network containing them must be trusted and secure, and deployers are told to think carefully about that before use. Cryptographic authentication of the remote ID is encouraged but out of scope. The RFC also warns that automatically re-broadcasting upstream DHCP broadcasts back downstream would let any public host spoof the DHCP server.
sections.eli5: This only works if the post office staff and the sorting room are honest. The stamps stop people from pretending to be someone else, but the system cannot protect itself from dishonest staff.

sections.title: IANA Registry for Sub-options
sections.content: IANA is required to maintain a new number space of DHCP Relay Agent Sub-options in the BOOTP-DHCP Parameters Registry, starting with the two sub-options defined here. Future sub-options are assigned under an IETF Consensus policy as described in RFC 2434. Drafts that propose new sub-options refer to them symbolically, and IANA assigns numeric codes only when they are approved for publication as an RFC.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of sub-option numbers, and a new number is only handed out once the community agrees it is worth having.
